title: The shield and the judge
hook: a well-known report: Ali loses a case against a Christian over a shield, because he has no witness, and the man becomes Muslim

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kharijites, who went out and declared others unbelievers. Your line was not our place to declare. Did you stop at a label and talk about the action instead? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

A stall in the market of Kufa, and on it, for sale, a piece of battle gear. A man walking past stops. He knows it. It's his. It went missing, and here it is, in the hands of a Christian trader. The man walking past is Ali, commander of the faithful, ruler of the Muslims. He could have it taken with a word. Instead, the story goes, he says: let's go to the judge. This is a well-known report, and it is worth hearing carefully, because it is more about the judge than the shield. Today, a courtroom.
screen: `A STALL IN KUFA.` → `THAT'S MINE.` → `LET'S GO TO THE JUDGE.`

segments.voice: The judge is Shurayh, appointed by the caliphs. The caliph walks in as an ordinary party to a case, and in some tellings he gently objects when Shurayh shows him more respect than the other man. The claim is simple. Ali says: it's mine. The trader says: it's mine, and it's in my hand. Shurayh turns to Ali. Do you have witnesses? Ali brings his son Hasan, and in some tellings his servant Qanbar too. And the judge says, in the telling, that he will not accept a son's testimony for his father. Ali has no further proof. So Shurayh rules for the trader. The caliph lost the case, before his own judge, in his own city. The trader walks out with the gear, and then turns back. The ruler of the Muslims, he says, brought me before his own judge, and the judge ruled against him. He says the gear really is Ali's, that it fell from his camel on the road, and he declares himself a Muslim. In the story, Ali gives it to him as a gift. Now the careful part. The report is found in later collections, such as al-Bayhaqi's, and hadith scholars have questioned the strength of its chain. Some tellings make the trader a Jewish man rather than a Christian. And the gear is often a coat of mail rather than a shield. So it is best heard as a report the tradition loves, not a sealed record. What it keeps alive is a command the Qur'an gives: when you judge between people, judge with justice. Shurayh did, even with the caliph standing before him. A ruler who loses fairly in his own court.
screen: `THE CALIPH AS AN ORDINARY PARTY.` · `NO SON'S TESTIMONY FOR HIS FATHER.` · `THE TRADER TURNS BACK.` · `A LOVED REPORT, A QUESTIONED CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE CALIPH LOST THE CASE.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept a fair ruling against you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time recently when a decision went against you, and the process was fair. A referee's call. A review at work. A vote in the family. A friend who said, honestly, you were wrong there. Breathe in, and notice whether any part of you is still arguing the case. Breathe out, and let the ruling stand. You can be sure you were right and still honor a fair process. If you pray, you can ask for a just heart. The bell holds the time.

The shield and the judge. A well-known report in which Ali, as caliph, loses a case before the judge Shurayh for lack of a witness, and the other man, moved by the fairness, becomes Muslim. Today's word.
screen: `THE SHIELD AND THE JUDGE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the caliph lost the case. Today, if you hold any power over someone, a parent, a boss, a team lead, let one decision go to them on its merits, even when you could overrule it. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the report of Ali and the judge Shurayh when teaching that rulers stand equal before the law, while noting that hadith scholars have questioned its chain.

fork.setup: you're the judge. the caliph who appointed you claims the gear. his only witness is his son. what do you rule?
options: for the caliph; who would doubt him?
for the trader; the caliph has no acceptable witness.
fork.reveal: in the report, Shurayh rules for the trader, and the caliph accepts it.

original.note: Arabic: a judge; Shurayh was the qadi of Kufa in this report.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a lost shield.
what it means: a ruler who loses fairly in his own court, and a man moved by that fairness.
what a scholar hears: a report in later collections with a questioned chain, variants that make the trader Christian or Jewish, and gear often named as a coat of mail.

sources.ref: al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra (Ali and Shurayh: the case over the armor)

notes: Audit: 'Ali has no other proof' contradicted the tellings in which Qanbar also testifies; the teach now mentions Qanbar in some tellings and says Ali had no further proof (one witness short).
The report's chain is weak by many hadith scholars' assessment; the script says so and calls it 'a report the tradition loves'. Confirm phrasing and the source references (al-Bayhaqi, Abu Nu'aym).

Variants: the trader is Christian in some tellings and Jewish in others; the item is usually dir' (coat of mail). The index says 'shield' and 'Christian'; the script follows the index and notes the variants. Consider renaming the index word to 'the armor and the judge'.
Some versions name Qanbar as a second witness whom Shurayh accepts, leaving Ali one witness short; the script simplifies to Hasan only. Confirm.
The conversion is told without framing it against Christianity; confirm the tone is welcoming to Christian listeners.
The hook calls it 'a well-known report', following the index.

Editor: Qur'an 4:135 was already the closing verse of day 874 (the Coptic boy), so the teach now paraphrases 4:58 (judge between people with justice), which also fits a story about a judge; source updated. Practice line no longer tells the listener what they feel.
